## How they got there
Inter reached the final as runners-up after losing to Paris Saint-Germain with a scoreline of 0-5. Their campaign was defined by an elite profile, particularly in Points per game at 2.38 where they performed better than 94% of teams in their group phase and 91% historically, alongside Opponent shots on target per game at 2.9 which placed them ahead of 89% of peers in the same season and 90% over the long term. This defensive solidity was complemented by a Goal difference per game of 1.25, a metric where they finished better than 88% of teams during their group stage and 83% across all Champions League history since 2011-12.

## Would the model have picked them?
The model would not have selected Inter for the final, as their probability ranking of 7 placed them outside its top two choices despite a 12.9% chance of reaching the summit compared to an 8.3% base rate for random knockout teams. Although this probability ranked seventh among all participants, the algorithm's expectation was closest to the quarter-finals with a score of 0.87 on its specific scale. Consequently, while Inter exceeded the average likelihood of advancement, their overall statistical profile did not meet the model's strict criteria for selection given the competition they faced in that season.

## Weak spots
Inter struggled significantly in Distance covered per game at 68.1 km, a figure where they performed better than only 3% of teams in their group phase and 0% historically. Their Shot accuracy (% on target) was similarly low at 39.2%, allowing them to beat just 8% of teams during the season and 12% over the long term. Additionally, their Attacks per game stood at 38.4, a rate that saw them outperform only 35% of peers in the group stage and 46% across all Champions League data since 2011-12.

messages.content: You are a football performance analyst writing for a curious, data-literate reader. Use ONLY the facts provided. Quote every number exactly as it appears in the facts, with the same rounding. Do not introduce players, managers, matches, events, analyses or numbers that are not in the facts. 'Teams beaten (%)' figures say how many teams the club did better than on a stat, so higher is always better, including for stats marked '(lower is better)', where doing better means having the lower value. Write them as 'better than X% of teams', never as 'top X%'. SHAP contributions are measured in knockout stages: a positive contribution means the stat pushed the model's expected stage up by that fraction of a round, a negative one pushed it down. A SHAP contribution is the model's view, not a measure of how good the team was at the stat: a team can rank high on a stat the model marked down, so never call a stat a strength or a weakness because of its SHAP sign. Everything here is a statistical association, not a cause: never say a stat or a team's profile drove, powered, propelled, carried, helped, hindered or prevented a result, and do not explain why a stat got its contribution. Write plain markdown without tables.
